title: Topic 10 Resource provision - Hodder practice questions

questions.question_text: Figure 10.40 shows the daily supply of calories in relation to GNP. State the approximate calorie intake for the USA and for Niger.

marking_scheme.rubric: Award 1 mark each for USA (c. 3800 kcal) and Niger (c. 2600 kcal). Max 2 marks.

questions.question_text: Describe the relationship between calorie intake and GDP per capita as shown on the graph.

points: There is a positive relationship / correlation: as GDP per capita increases, daily calorie intake increases [1]
Comparative evidence: USA has high GDP per head (c. $60,000) and high calorie intake (c. 3800 kcal), whereas low GDP countries like India (GDP < $10,000) have lower intake (c. 2500–2600 kcal) [1]
Anomalies exist: e.g. Kiribati and Niger have low GDP per capita but higher-than-expected calorie intake, or intake plateaus at high income levels [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 3 marks: 1 mark for stating positive correlation, 1 mark for supporting data/examples, 1 mark for identifying anomalies.

questions.question_text: Explain one human factor and one physical factor that negatively affects food supply.

points: Human factor: Rapid population growth / overpopulation increasing food demand beyond local agricultural capacity [1], leading to food shortages and unequal distribution [1]; OR: War / armed conflict displacing farmers, destroying crops, and blocking food transport routes [1-2]; OR: Poverty preventing farmers from purchasing fertilisers, seeds, and machinery [1-2]

Physical factor: Drought / erratic rainfall depriving crops of moisture, causing crop failure and livestock death [1-2]; OR: Extreme pests / diseases (e.g. locust swarms, fungal blight) wiping out harvests [1-2]; OR: Soil degradation / desertification reducing arable land fertility [1-2]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award 2 marks for the human factor (1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation) and 2 marks for the physical factor. Max 4 marks.

questions.question_text: Explain two ways in which food production can be increased.

points: Way 1: Increased use of synthetic or organic fertilisers to replenish essential soil nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus), accelerating plant growth and multiplying crop yields [2]
Way 2: Modern irrigation systems (e.g. drip irrigation, center-pivot) supplying reliable water to crops in arid regions or during dry seasons, allowing multiple harvests per year [2]

Alternative ways: Genetically modified (GM) or High-Yielding Variety (HYV) seeds bred for pest/drought resistance; Mechanisation (tractors, combine harvesters) increasing farming efficiency; Hydroponics / vertical farming [2 marks each]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award 2 marks for each well-explained method (1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation of how it increases yield). Max 4 marks.

questions.question_text: Figure 10.41 shows the world's different fuel sources. Calculate the change in the size of the world's fuel sources between 1970 and 2030 (predicted).

points: Overall increase: an increase of 350 Tj (or an increase of c. 256%, accept 240–265%) [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 3 marks: 1 mark for 1970 figure, 1 mark for 2030 figure, 1 mark for calculation of difference or percentage increase.

questions.question_text: Identify the fuel source that is predicted to have increased most in absolute size, and the fuel source that is predicted to have increased most in relative size between 1970 and 2030.

points: Increased most in absolute size: Oil (or natural gas) [1]
Increased most in relative size / percentage growth: Nuclear power [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award 1 mark for absolute increase (oil/gas) and 1 mark for relative increase (nuclear). Max 2 marks.

questions.question_text: Assess the advantages and disadvantages of different types of energy sources.

inputs.label: Nhập bài làm Case Study (7 marks):

points: Non-renewable fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas): Advantages — high energy density, reliable base-load power, existing transport and generation infrastructure. Disadvantages — finite/depleting reserves, greenhouse gas emissions driving climate change, air pollution (SO₂, particulate smog) [2-3 marks]

Renewable energy (solar, wind, HEP, geothermal): Advantages — inexhaustible/sustainable, zero operational greenhouse gas emissions, falling technology costs. Disadvantages — intermittent/weather-dependent, geographic restrictions, visual and noise impacts, high initial capital investment [2-3 marks]
Nuclear power: High energy output with low direct emissions, but produces hazardous radioactive waste and carries catastrophic risk (Chernobyl, Fukushima) [1-2 marks]

Assessment / Evaluation: Judging the future energy transition mix, concluding that while non-renewables currently dominate, a diversified transition to renewables supported by smart grids and storage is essential [1 mark]
marking_scheme.rubric: Level 1 (1-3 marks): Simple descriptions of energy types without clear categorization of pros and cons. Level 2 (4-6 marks): Detailed explanation of advantages and disadvantages of both renewable and non-renewable sources with examples. Level 3 (7 marks): Comprehensive and balanced assessment comparing energy sources, weighing environmental impacts against economic reliability, supported by named examples, arriving at a well-reasoned conclusion.
